title: Greetings and introductions: bonjour, je m'appelle
summary: Say hello and goodbye, choose tu or vous, give your name with je m'appelle, and say please and thank you.
focus: Greeting people politely and introducing yourself
content:
## Hello and goodbye

French greetings change with the time of day and with the person in front of you.

| French | Use it… |
|---|---|
| **bonjour** | hello, good morning (all day, to anyone) |
| **bonsoir** | good evening (from about 6 p.m.) |
| **salut** | hi, bye (friends and family only) |
| **au revoir** | goodbye (to anyone) |

When you leave, add **bonne journée** (have a good day), **à bientôt** (see you soon) or **à demain** (see you tomorrow). To ask how someone is, say **Ça va ?** The usual answer is **Ça va bien, merci.** (I'm fine, thanks.)

> **Bonjour first.** Say **bonjour** before anything else, whether you are entering a shop, getting on a bus or asking the way. Starting straight with your question sounds rude. Add **monsieur** or **madame**: **Bonjour, madame.**

## Tu or vous?

French has two words for *you*.

- **tu**: one person you know well, such as a friend, a relative, a child or a classmate.
- **vous**: one person you don't know, or someone older or senior (a shop assistant, a doctor, your boss); and **always** more than one person, friends included.

When in doubt, use **vous** and let the other person suggest **tu**. With **tu** you say **salut** and **s'il te plaît**; with **vous**, **bonjour** and **s'il vous plaît**.

## Je m'appelle: saying your name

**S'appeler** (to be called) gives your name. It is *reflexive*: a small pronoun sits before the verb, and **me, te, se** become **m', t', s'** before the vowel.

| | s'appeler |
|---|---|
| je | **m'appelle** |
| tu | **t'appelles** |
| il / elle / on | **s'appelle** |
| nous | **nous appelons** |
| vous | **vous appelez** |
| ils / elles | **s'appellent** |

Spelling: **ll** where the ending is silent (*appelle, appelles, appellent*), one **l** in *appelons, appelez*.

- **Comment tu t'appelles ?** What's your name? (tu)
- **Comment vous appelez-vous ?** What's your name? (vous)
- **Enchanté.** Pleased to meet you. A woman writes **enchantée**; it sounds the same.

## Polite words

- **merci** (thank you), **merci beaucoup** (thank you very much)
- **de rien** (you're welcome); more formal: **je vous en prie**
- **s'il vous plaît** (please, to **vous**), **s'il te plaît** (to **tu**)
- **oui** (yes), **non** (no), **pardon** (sorry, excuse me)
- **monsieur** (sir, Mr), **madame** (madam, Mrs, Ms)

**Merci, monsieur. Au revoir, madame. Bonne journée !**

vocabulary.example_meaning: Good evening, sir, how are you?
Goodbye, and have a good day!

vocabulary.meaning: how are you?, how's it going?
vocabulary.example: Ça va ? — Oui, ça va bien, merci.
vocabulary.example_meaning: How are you? — Yes, I'm fine, thanks.

vocabulary.meaning: to be called (to give one's name)

vocabulary.example_meaning: Pleased to meet you, my name is Claire.

quiz.prompt: It's 8 p.m. and you walk into a restaurant. You say…
quiz.explanation: From about 6 p.m. the greeting is bonsoir. Bonne nuit is only said when someone goes to bed, and salut is too casual for a stranger.

quiz.prompt: You meet your friend's grandmother for the first time. How do you ask her name?
quiz.explanation: An older person you have just met gets vous: Comment vous appelez-vous ? Comment elle s'appelle ? asks about someone else.
hints: Stranger and older: tu or vous?

quiz.prompt: You say Merci to a shop assistant. She answers…
quiz.explanation: De rien (you're welcome) is the reply to merci. Enchantée is for meeting someone, s'il vous plaît for asking.
Il and elle take s'appelle: Elle s'appelle Camille. M'appelle goes with je, t'appelles with tu.
hints: Elle, like il, takes se: s'.

quiz.explanation: With je, s'appeler is m'appelle: Je m'appelle Lucas. Me becomes m' before the vowel.
hints: Reflexive pronoun for je, then the verb.
Two l's: the ending is silent.

quiz.explanation: Vous takes -ez, and the stem keeps one l because the ending is heard: vous vous appelez.

quiz.prompt: At the bakery: Une baguette, ___, madame. (please)
quiz.explanation: To a shop assistant you use vous, so please is s'il vous plaît.
hints: A stranger in a shop: tu or vous?

quiz.prompt: In France, you say bonjour before asking a shop assistant for anything.
quiz.explanation: True. Bonjour comes first every time, whether in a shop, on a bus or before asking the way. Skipping it sounds rude.
hints: Think of the politeness rule in the first section.

quiz.prompt: Salut is a good greeting for a job interview.
quiz.explanation: False. Salut is for friends and family. An interviewer gets Bonjour, madame or Bonjour, monsieur, and vous.

conversations.title: On the stairs
conversations.scenario: Hugo, a student, meets his new neighbour Hélène Martin on the stairs of their building.

lines.speaker: a
lines.note: She says vous because they have just met.

lines.speaker: b
lines.meaning: My name is Hugo. And you?

lines.speaker: a
lines.meaning: My name is Hélène Martin. Pleased to meet you!

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui, ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?
lines.meaning: Yes, I'm fine, thanks. And you?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Très bien, merci. Bonne journée, Hugo !
lines.meaning: Very well, thanks. Have a good day, Hugo!

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Merci, vous aussi ! Au revoir, madame.

listening.meaning: Thank you very much, sir. You're welcome!
Good evening, madam. What's your name?

listening.text: Il s'appelle Karim, et elle s'appelle Inès.
listening.meaning: His name is Karim, and her name is Inès.

listening.text: Enchanté, madame, je m'appelle Thomas. Et vous ?
listening.meaning: Pleased to meet you, madam, my name is Thomas. And you?

listening.text: Un thé, s'il vous plaît, monsieur. Merci, bonne journée !
listening.meaning: A tea, please, sir. Thanks, have a good day!
listening.note: New word: un thé = a tea.

listening.text: Nous nous appelons Dubois, et nos enfants s'appellent Jules et Rose.
listening.meaning: Our name is Dubois, and our children are called Jules and Rose.
listening.note: New word: nos enfants = our children.

guide.tip: Say bonjour first, every time. People respond much more helpfully when you do.

concept.title: La bise or a handshake?
concept.markdown: Friends and family often greet with **la bise**, a light kiss on each cheek; how many depends on the region. At work, people shake hands. The words come either way: **Salut, ça va ?** with a bise, **Bonjour, enchanté** with a handshake.

bites.title: Bonjour first
bites.rule: Say bonjour (bonsoir after about 6 p.m.) before anything else, in a shop, on a bus or when asking the way. Salut is for friends only.
bites.example: Bonjour, madame. Un café, s'il vous plaît.

bites.title: Tu or vous
bites.rule: Use tu for one friend, relative or child. Use vous for a stranger, someone senior, or any group. When in doubt, use vous.
bites.example: Tu t'appelles comment ? Vous vous appelez comment ?
bites.example_meaning: What's your name? (to a friend) What's your name? (polite)

bites.title: Je m'appelle
bites.rule: S'appeler gives your name: je m'appelle, tu t'appelles, il s'appelle, nous nous appelons, vous vous appelez, ils s'appellent.
bites.example_meaning: My name is Inès. And you?

bites.title: Thanks and please
bites.rule: Say merci, and de rien in reply. Use s'il vous plaît to vous and s'il te plaît to tu. Say enchanté(e) when you meet someone.

sorts.title: Tu or vous?
sorts.why: Tu is for one person you know well; vous is for strangers, people senior to you, and any group, even of friends.

sorts.title: Arriving or leaving?
sorts.why: Bonjour, enchanté and ça va open a meeting; au revoir, bonne journée, à bientôt and à demain close it.

spots.why: With tu the verb ends in -es: tu t'appelles.
Salut is for friends; a director gets bonjour.
With je the pronoun is me: je m'appelle.
